title: Why cities are rethinking their night-time economies

blocks.text: For decades, city centres emptied out after the last train. Now a growing number of municipalities are treating the night as an economy in its own right, with dedicated officials, licensing rules and public transport timetables built around bars, clubs and late-shift workers.

The idea is not new. Amsterdam appointed a night mayor more than a decade ago, and several European cities followed. What has changed is the scope: the role now often covers noise complaints, safety, waste collection and the interests of people who work while everyone else sleeps.

Critics say the title flatters a narrow group of venue owners. Residents' associations argue that a night-time economy policy should start with sleep, not with opening hours. Both sides agree that the old approach, which treated nightlife mainly as a policing problem, did not work.

blocks.caption: Late-night workers are often left out of consultations.

blocks.text: Who counts as a night worker?

Cleaners, nurses, delivery drivers and security staff all work at night, but they rarely appear in the same meetings as club owners. Some cities now reserve seats on night-time boards for unions and hospital staff, arguing that a policy built only around leisure will miss most of the people affected.

blocks.text: The results are mixed. Transport improvements are popular, while noise rules remain contested. Officials say the point is not to make everyone agree, but to give the argument a regular place to happen.
